content.title: About
content.content: A chimichanga is a deep‑fried or baked Mexican dish consisting of a flour tortilla filled with meat, cheese, beans and spices. The dough is usually made from wheat flour, water, eggs and salt, while the filling can include beef, pork or chicken seasoned with chili, cumin and other aromatic spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chimichanga originated in the American Southwest where Mexican cuisine merged with local Indigenous cooking traditions.
Traditionally the dish was cooked in clay pots, but modern restaurants often use deep fryers.
There is a seafood version where meat is replaced by shrimp or fish.
In the United States chimichangas are commonly served with salsa, guacamole and sour cream.
The name comes from the Spanish word “chimichanga,” which, according to one theory, is a corruption of the English phrase “cheese change.”

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef and pork are good sources of heme iron, supporting normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and spices supply vitamins B12, B6 and niacin, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Provides fiber (when beans are added)
items.content: Beans in the filling increase dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Fried chimichangas can be high in saturated fat and calories; moderation is advised.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor pathogens; ensure internal temperature reaches at least 71 °C.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat flour tortilla contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Chili and other spices can irritate the stomach in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the chimichanga hot, cut into wedges. It can be eaten with hands like a taco or with a fork and knife. Common accompaniments are salsa, guacamole, sour cream, lime wedges and fresh cilantro.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chimichanga in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 71 °C before serving.
